newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Anesta sees 97 FDA OK for Actiq.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Anesta sees 97 FDA OK for Actiq.

text.p: Anesta Corp's Chief Executive William Moeller said the company expects the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to approve its oral transmucosal Actiq product for cancer pain for marketing by late 1997.

Moeller declined to comment on specific earnings projections, but said future sales revenues would be "very much dependent" on Actiq and added that analysts' forecasts that said the company could break even by the fourth quarter of 1998 "are pretty close to what we would think."

"We estimate the FDA will probably approve it in six to 12 months," Moeller said in an interview with Reuters. "This drug falls into the category of dealing with cancer and the FDA has a policy of expediting approval."

Anesta submitted a New Drug Application for Actiq in November for the treatment of "breakthrough" pain in cancer patients -- pain that breaks through a constant pain level classified as "moderate to severe" by the World Health Organization.

Breakthrough pain is reported in more than 50 percent of cancer patients and it can occur one to four times daily, tending to reach maximal intensity in three minutes and lasting for an average of 30 minutes.

Moderate to severe cancer pain is currently treated with drugs known as opiods, such as morphine and Fentanyl patch treatements which, if ramped up to deal with breakthrough pain, could cause side effects, he said.

Actiq, also Fentanyl-based, is used in conjunction with the steady-state pain treatments and is absorbed through the walls of the mouth through an oral transmucosal delivery system that allows for quick effect, he said.
Other products in the pipeline are a smoking-cessation product, which is in its Phase II clinical stage. It involves using nicotine with a similar oral delivery system.
Moeller said he does not see the company filing a New Drug Application for this product within the year, but was working towards it.
If the product was targeted at the over-the-counter market, it would require teaming up with a partner who could provide the necessary marketing, he said.

In the more preliminary Phase I stage is an ultra short-acting sedative product called OT-Etomidate which also uses the oral transmucosal delivery method. Etomidate is an approved drug currently in use for intravenous sedation.

The company's first product, Fentanyl Oralet, is FDA approved and is being marketed by Abbott Laboratories as a sedative and analgesic before painful procedures that do not warrant general anaesthetic.
Abbott also manufactures and intends to market Actiq under license from Anesta in the United States.
Moellet said Anesta is working toward partnering with other companies internationally. He said it was in discussions with a number of parties, but had reached no agreement as yet.
